Part 0 · Toolkit · Chapter 0.7

Probability and statistics

How to read a model's probabilities and losses, and how much a test score varies by chance

A classifier usually outputs probabilities, training minimises a loss built from them, and a test score changes with the test set. This chapter covers mean and spread, the normal curve, base rates, softmax, cross-entropy and moving averages, then resampling, confidence intervals and tests of whether a score gap could be luck. It ends with correlation: two columns can move together without one driving the other.

You will need: exponents and logarithms for softmax and cross-entropy, and the idea of a slope from 0.6. Vectors (0.5) appear once, in the correlation section.

Mean and spread

Guess first. Nine spadenose sharks from the made-up catch records measure between 33 and 48 cm. A typing slip turns 48.3 cm into 95 cm. Does the mean rise by about 0.5 cm, 5 cm or 50 cm? Does the median, the middle value, move?

The mean \(\bar{x}\) of \(n\) values is their sum divided by \(n\), and it locates their centre. A deviation is a value minus the mean, so its size says how far the value lies from that centre and its sign says on which side. The variance \(\sigma^2\) is the average of the squared deviations. The standard deviation (SD) \(\sigma\) is its square root, which has the unit of the data. Squaring gives large deviations more weight than small ones. So one outlier, a value far from the rest, can raise the SD by much more than it raises the mean.

  1. Dots are lengths, the teal line is the mean, coral segments are deviations, the sand marker is the median and the band reaches one SD either side of the mean. Press “Add a typing slip: 48.3 becomes 95” and read the three boxes under the plot.
  2. Press “Reset”, then drag any dot, or focus it and press the arrow keys. The mean and the SD change as the dot moves, but the median changes only when the dot is the middle one or crosses the sand marker.
Mean 0 cmMedian 0 cmSD 0 cm

One typing slip lifts the mean from 37.2 to 42.4 cm and the SD from 5.1 to 18.9 cm, while the median stays at 35.4 cm.

How it works

Take three of the lengths: 33.2, 35.4 and 44.1 cm. Their mean is 37.57 cm, so the deviations are −4.37, −2.17 and 6.53 cm. The squared deviations, from the unrounded deviations, are 19.07, 4.69 and 42.68 cm2, and they add up to 66.45 cm2.

66.45sum of squared deviations, cm2÷3n, the number of lengths=22.15variance σ2, cm2→ square root →4.71SD σ, cm

Averaging the deviations directly would give 0, because the deviations from the mean add up to 0. Squaring removes the sign, and the square root returns the unit to cm. In the figure, the slipped length lies 52.6 cm above the new mean. Its squared deviation, about 2,760 cm2, is 86% of the new sum of squared deviations, 3,208 cm2, which is why the SD rises so much.

Common belief. The mean describes a typical shark.

Why it fails. After the slip, seven of the nine lengths lie between 32.7 and 37.3 cm, yet the mean is 42.4 cm, above all seven.

Better account. Report the mean with a spread, look at the values, and compare the mean with the median. The median is the middle value of the sorted list, so moving the largest value further out leaves it at 35.4 cm. A large gap between the two can signal outliers.

Quick quiz

The values 2, 4 and 6 have mean 4. What are their variance and SD?

The deviations are −2, 0 and 2, their squares are 4, 0 and 4, and these add up to 8. The variance is 8/3 = 2.67 and the SD is \(\sqrt{2.67}\) = 1.63.

When would you report the median instead of the mean?

When a few extreme values pull the mean away from where most of the data lies, as with a typing slip or with incomes in a city.

Mean or median

The median is the middle value of the sorted list, so it ignores how far the extremes go. That makes it steadier than the mean, and it gives no information about spread.

The whole catch table shows the same gap between mean and median. Its weights have a mean of 1.185 kg and a median of 0.43 kg. The 57 hammerheads and 3 Ganges sharks, with mean weights of 4.45 and 38 kg, pull the mean up.

Symbols

\[ \bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \qquad \sigma^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_i-\bar{x}\right)^2 \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2} \]

  • \(x_i\) is the \(i\)-th value (a shark's length) and \(n\) the number of values.
  • \(\bar{x}\), read "x bar", is the mean. \(\sigma^2\) is the variance and \(\sigma\) the standard deviation. The sigmoid is also written \(\sigma\), but it always has a bracket, \(\sigma(z)\).

Checks by hand

For the three lengths of the example, dividing by 2 instead of 3, as for a sample, would give an SD of 5.76 cm. The mean is the value that makes the sum of squared deviations smallest. For the nine lengths that sum is 235.8 about the mean of 37.23, against 266.0 about the median of 35.4 and 304.7 about 40.

In Python

import numpy as np

# nine spadenose lengths in cm, from the made-up catch records
lengths = np.array([32.7, 33.2, 33.4, 33.9, 35.4, 36.8, 37.3, 44.1, 48.3])
print("mean   :", round(lengths.mean(), 2))
print("median :", np.median(lengths))
print("SD     :", round(lengths.std(), 2), "(divides by n)")
print("SD     :", round(lengths.std(ddof=1), 2), "(divides by n - 1)")

lengths[-1] = 95                    # a typing slip
print("after the slip:", round(lengths.mean(), 2), round(lengths.std(), 2), np.median(lengths))

Common mistakes

Debug tip. NumPy's std divides by \(n\) unless you pass ddof=1. Dividing by \(n-1\) is the usual choice when the data is a sample used to estimate a larger group, and the two agree closely for large \(n\). Pandas divides by \(n-1\) by default, so the same column can give two answers in two libraries.

In practice

Quote the mean with the SD for a column that roughly follows a bell curve, and the median with the quartiles for a lopsided one. Pandas describe() prints the count, mean, SD, minimum, quartiles and maximum in one table. A glance at it catches slips such as 95 cm for a spadenose shark.

Where this is used

Used in: checking data before training (B8), and the spread of a test score (sections below).

More questions

Why does the SD react more to one outlier than the mean does?

The SD squares the deviations, so a deviation twice as large counts four times as much. The mean only adds the values.

What is the SD of the values 5, 5, 5 and 5?

It is 0. All the deviations are 0, so the variance is 0. A column with an SD of 0 gives a model no information.

The normal curve and z-scores

Guess first. The 268 made-up spadenose lengths average 39 cm with an SD of 8.6 cm. About what share of the sharks lie within 8.6 cm of the average: one half, two thirds or nearly all?

A normal distribution is the bell curve set by a mean \(\mu\) and an SD \(\sigma\). For a column whose histogram is close to a normal distribution, about 68% of the values lie within one SD of \(\mu\) and about 95% within two. The z-score of a value \(x\) is \(z = (x-\mu)/\sigma\), the number of SDs between \(x\) and the mean, negative below the mean. Standardising a column replaces all its values by z-scores computed with its own mean and SD, so it has mean 0 and SD 1 whatever its unit.

  1. The bars are the 268 lengths and the coral curve is the normal curve for the \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) on the sliders. At \(\mu\) = 39.1 and \(\sigma\) = 8.6 cm the line under the plot reads 65.7% of the sharks within one SD, against 68.3% for the curve.
  2. Move the slider for \(x\): the boxes under the plot compute \(z\) (1.51 at \(x\) = 52.1 cm). Press “Standardised (z-scores)” and the axis counts SDs.
  3. Press “Original units”, then choose “Weight, kg” and the bars are tallest between 0.06 and 0.17 kg, while the curve extends below 0 kg.
Column

About 66% of the lengths fall within one SD, close to the normal curve's 68%, but for weights the curve extends below 0 kg.

How it works

Take a spadenose shark of length \(x\) = 52.1 cm. With \(\mu\) = 39.1 cm and \(\sigma\) = 8.6 cm, its z-score is \(z\) = (52.1 − 39.1)/8.6 = 13.0/8.6 = 1.51.

52.1 − 39.1 = 13.0x − μ, the value minus the mean, cm÷8.6σ, the SD, cm=1.51z, the z-score: 1.51 SDs above the mean

Subtracting \(\mu\) moves the centre of the column to 0, and dividing by \(\sigma\) makes one SD the unit. Length in cm, girth (the distance around the body) in cm and weight in kg then all count in SDs, which puts the columns on one scale.

Common belief. Measurements follow a bell curve.

Why it fails. In this table weight follows roughly the cube of the length, so the 268 spadenose weights are mostly small, with a long tail of large weights. The normal curve with the mean and SD of the weights puts about 5% of its area below 0 kg.

Better account. Look at the histogram first. Any column with an SD above 0 can be standardised. The shares of 68% within one SD and 95% within two apply to columns close to a bell curve.

Quick quiz

Spadenose lengths have mean 39.1 cm and SD 8.6 cm. A shark has \(z = -2\). How long is it?

\(x = \mu + z\sigma = 39.1 - 2\times8.6 = 21.9\) cm. Only about 2.3% of a bell curve lies that far below the mean.

After standardising, what are the mean and SD of the column, and why does that put length in cm and weight in kg on one scale?

The mean is 0 and the SD is 1, whatever the original unit. A value then counts in SDs from the mean of its own column, so the unit (cm or kg) drops out.

A term: density

density
the height of the curve: the area under it is a probability

Reading the figure

The bars show the 268 spadenose sharks of the made-up catch records, grouped into bins. Their height is the share of sharks in the bin divided by the bin width, so that the bars and the curve use the same density axis. The coral curve is the normal curve for the \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) you choose, with the darker band for one SD and the lighter for two. "Fit to the data" sets \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) to the column's own mean and SD. Now switch to the standardised view. A value \(x\) becomes \(z = (x-\mu)/\sigma\), so with the fitted numbers the histogram is drawn on the same scale whether the column is in centimetres or kilograms. For length it stays close to the standard curve (65.7% within one SD against 68.3%), and for weight it does not. Drag the sliders away from the fit and the histogram moves away from the curve.

Standardising matters for training. Length runs from 20 to 60 and weight from 0.02 to 0.8, so a model that adds them up mixes very different scales. A2 uses z-scores for feature scaling, and batch norm in B6 standardises numbers inside a network.

Symbols

\[ z = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \qquad f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\;e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)} \]

  • \(\mu\) is the mean and \(\sigma\) the SD of the column (for a sample, the sample mean and SD).
  • \(f(x)\) is the height of the normal curve at \(x\). You rarely compute it by hand; the useful facts are the shares: 68.3% of the area within one SD, 95.4% within two, 99.7% within three.

A z-score depends on the group

A z-score depends on the group you standardise against. Tag 5519 is an 82.0 cm hammerhead in the made-up catch records. Among all 600 records (mean 54.0 cm, SD 22.8 cm) it has \(z = (82.0-54.0)/22.8 = 1.23\), so it looks long. Among the 57 hammerheads (mean 82.1 cm, SD 41.4 cm) its z-score is about 0, because it is a typical hammerhead.

Lopsided columns

Counts, waiting times and incomes are often lopsided as well.

A quick estimate from the curve

The bell curve also gives a quick estimate. A spadenose shark of 50 cm has \(z = (50-39.1)/8.6 = 1.27\), and about 10.2% of a bell curve lies above that. The made-up table has 30 spadenose sharks above 50 cm out of 268, which is 11.2%. The two differ by one percentage point, so at this threshold the bell curve gives a close estimate, as the 66% within one SD suggested.

In Python

import numpy as np

# the same nine sharks from the made-up catch records
length = np.array([32.7, 33.2, 33.4, 33.9, 35.4, 36.8, 37.3, 44.1, 48.3])        # cm
weight = np.array([0.101, 0.128, 0.118, 0.122, 0.144, 0.156, 0.145, 0.331, 0.316])  # kg

def standardise(column, mean=None, std=None):
    mean = column.mean() if mean is None else mean
    std = column.std() if std is None else std
    return (column - mean) / std

zl, zw = standardise(length), standardise(weight)
print("length z:", zl.round(2))
print("weight z:", zw.round(2))
print("means about 0:", np.allclose([zl.mean(), zw.mean()], 0), " SDs:", zl.std().round(2), zw.std().round(2))

new_shark = np.array([52.0])        # new data: reuse the old mean and SD
print("z of a 52 cm shark:", standardise(new_shark, length.mean(), length.std()).round(2))
length z: [-0.89 -0.79 -0.75 -0.65 -0.36 -0.08  0.01  1.34  2.16]
weight z: [-0.89 -0.56 -0.68 -0.63 -0.36 -0.21 -0.35  1.93  1.74]
means about 0: True  SDs: 1.0 1.0
z of a 52 cm shark: [2.88]
from math import erf, sqrt

# Tag 5519: an 82.0 cm hammerhead, made-up record
z_all = (82.0 - 53.98) / 22.77       # against all 600 records
z_own = (82.0 - 82.11) / 41.4        # against the 57 hammerheads
print(round(z_all, 2), round(z_own, 3))

# share of spadenose sharks above 50 cm if lengths followed a bell curve
z = (50 - 39.1) / 8.6
share = 0.5 * (1 - erf(z / sqrt(2)))
print(round(z, 2), round(share, 3), "against", round(30 / 268, 3), "in the table")
1.23 -0.003
1.27 0.102 against 0.112 in the table

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Compute the mean and SD on the training data only, then reuse those same two numbers on validation and test data. Computing them on all the data lets test information reach the training features, and standardising the validation and test sets with their own numbers puts the sets on different scales and hides shifts in the data (A4).

In practice

A column whose values are all equal has an SD of 0 and divides by zero. Code either drops such a column or adds a tiny number \(\epsilon\) to the variance, as the normalisation layers of B6 do.

Where this is used

Used in: feature scaling (A2), batch norm and layer norm (B6), and the normal-curve intervals later in this chapter.

More questions

A shark is 52 cm long. Lengths have mean 39.1 and SD 8.6. What is its z-score, and is it unusual?

\(z = (52 - 39.1)/8.6 = 1.5\). That is 1.5 SDs above the mean, large but not rare: about 7% of a bell curve lies above it.

Base rates and Bayes' rule

Guess first. A made-up diabetes test flags 90% of the patients who have diabetes and clears 90% of those who do not. In one clinic 8 patients in 100 have diabetes, and a patient tests positive. How likely is it that this patient has diabetes: about 90%, about 50% or about 10%?

The base rate is the share of all patients who have the condition before any test, here 8%. The test has a sensitivity, the share of sick patients it flags (marks positive), and a specificity, the share of healthy patients it clears (marks negative). Bayes' rule turns these three numbers into the chance that a flagged patient is sick, which here differs from the sensitivity. A rare condition can make a good test flag more healthy than sick patients.

  1. A circle is a patient: coral with diabetes, navy without, filled if the test flagged the patient and a ring if not. Press “Only the flagged” and read the first row of boxes under the plot: 72 ÷ 164 = 43.9% of the filled circles are coral.
  2. Set the share of patients with diabetes to 1%, with sensitivity and specificity still 90%: the first row gives 9 ÷ 108 = 8.3%, because the 99 healthy patients flagged by mistake outnumber the 9 sick ones found.
Example
Show

At a base rate of 8%, a test with 90% sensitivity and 90% specificity flags 164 of 1,000 patients, and only 72 of them (44%) have diabetes.

How it works

Count 1,000 patients at a base rate of 8%: 80 are sick, and the test flags 90% of them, 72 patients. It clears 90% of the 920 healthy patients and flags the other 10%, 92 patients, so 164 patients are flagged and 72/164 = 44% of them are sick.

D means that the patient has diabetes and + that the test flags the patient. The bar in \(P(+ \mid D)\) reads “given”, so \(P(+ \mid D)\) = 0.90 is the chance of a flag given diabetes (the sensitivity). Likewise \(P(+ \mid \text{not } D)\) = 0.10 is 1 minus the specificity, and \(P(D \mid +)\) is the chance of diabetes given a flag. Also \(P(D)\) = 0.08 is the base rate, and \(P(+)\) = 0.072 + 0.092 = 0.164 is the chance that a patient is flagged.

0.08 × 0.90P(D) × P(+ | D): sick and flagged÷0.072 + 0.92 × 0.10P(+): all flagged patients=0.439P(D | +): chance a flagged patient is sick

Common belief. A test that is right 90% of the time makes a positive result 90% likely to be right.

Why it fails. The 90% is the share of sick patients that are flagged, but a flagged patient's chance of being sick is the share of flagged patients that are sick. At a base rate of 8% these two shares are 90% and 44%.

Better account. Count a population, split it by the base rate, apply the test, and look only at the flagged group.

Quick quiz

The same test is used where 35% of patients are sick. Does a flagged patient's chance of being sick rise or fall, and to what?

It rises, to about 83%: \(0.9 \times 0.35 = 0.315\) flagged and sick, against \(0.1 \times 0.65 = 0.065\) flagged and healthy, so \(0.315/0.380 = 0.83\).

Why can a test with 99% sensitivity and 95% specificity still give mostly false alarms when 1% of patients are sick?

If only 1% are sick, the 95% specificity still flags 5% of the 99% who are healthy. That is about 50 false alarms for 10 true cases.

A term: probability

probability
a number from 0 to 1 for how often something happens in the long run

Reading the figure

The figure draws 1,000 patients as circles and has four views (All patients, Who has diabetes, Test result, Only the flagged): step through them, then move the sliders. Sensitivity is the share of sick patients the test flags, and specificity is the share of healthy patients it clears (A4 grades models with both). In "Only the flagged", the question for a flagged patient is: of all the filled circles, how many are coral? With 8% prevalence the answer is 44%, because 92 of the 920 healthy patients are flagged by mistake, which is more than the 72 sick patients the test catches.

Two more examples

Try the second preset, “Pima women, glucose rule”. It uses a one-line rule on the Pima data: flag any woman whose glucose is 140 mg/dL or higher. The Pima data is a published dataset of 768 women of Pima heritage, measured in the United States, not data from Mumbai. Among the 763 women with a glucose reading, the rule flags 51% of those with diabetes and clears 88% of those without. With the Pima base rate of 268 of 768 women (34.9%), 69% of the flagged women have diabetes. In a population where few women have diabetes, the same rule would flag a smaller share who have it if its sensitivity and specificity stayed the same (they can differ between populations). The third preset, “Rare condition”, is a test that is 99% sensitive and 95% specific, with 1% prevalence. A flagged patient has only a 17% chance of having the condition.

Symbols

\[ P(D \mid +) = \frac{P(+ \mid D)\,P(D)}{P(+ \mid D)\,P(D) + P(+ \mid \text{not } D)\,P(\text{not } D)} \]

  • \(D\) means the patient has diabetes and \(+\) means the test flags them. \(P(D \mid +)\) reads "the probability of \(D\) given \(+\)".
  • \(P(D)\) is the base rate. \(P(+ \mid D)\) is the sensitivity. \(P(+ \mid \text{not } D)\) is 1 minus the specificity.
  • Counting 1,000 patients, as above, is the same calculation in whole numbers. Gigerenzer and Hoffrage (1995) argued that counts like these make Bayesian reasoning easier than percentages do.

The rule is counting done twice. The share of patients who are sick and flagged can be written as \(P(D)\,P(+\mid D)\) or as \(P(+)\,P(D\mid +)\). Setting these equal and dividing by \(P(+)\) gives \(P(D\mid +)\). The flagged group has two sources, the sick who are flagged and the healthy who are flagged, which is why \(P(+)\) is the sum in the denominator.

By hand: the Pima rule

Now the Pima rule, with a base rate of 0.349, a sensitivity of 0.508 and a specificity of 0.875. Sick and flagged: \(0.349\times0.508 = 0.177\). Healthy and flagged: \(0.651\times0.125 = 0.081\). So \(P(D\mid +) = 0.177/(0.177+0.081) = 0.685\), the 69% above. Use the same rule where only 5 patients in 100 are sick. The two products become \(0.0254\) and \(0.1188\), and the chance falls to \(0.0254/0.1442 = 0.176\). The rule is the same and the answer has changed, because the base rate changed.

In Python

n, prevalence, sensitivity, specificity = 1000, 0.08, 0.90, 0.90

sick = n * prevalence
healthy = n - sick
caught = sick * sensitivity                 # sick and flagged
false_alarms = healthy * (1 - specificity)  # healthy and flagged
print("flagged:", caught + false_alarms, " of which sick:", caught)
print("chance a flagged patient is sick:", round(caught / (caught + false_alarms), 3))

# the same answer straight from Bayes' rule
p = sensitivity * prevalence / (sensitivity * prevalence + (1 - specificity) * (1 - prevalence))
print("Bayes' rule:", round(p, 3))
flagged: 164.0  of which sick: 72.0
chance a flagged patient is sick: 0.439
Bayes' rule: 0.439
def flagged_sick(prevalence, sensitivity, specificity):
    caught = sensitivity * prevalence
    false_alarms = (1 - specificity) * (1 - prevalence)
    return caught / (caught + false_alarms)

print(round(flagged_sick(0.349, 0.508, 0.875), 3))   # Pima glucose rule
print(round(flagged_sick(0.05, 0.508, 0.875), 3))    # same rule, 5% sick
print(round(flagged_sick(0.001, 0.99, 0.99), 3))     # good test, rare condition
0.685
0.176
0.09

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If your answer to "how likely is the disease after a positive result" equals the test's sensitivity, you may have swapped \(P(+ \mid D)\) and \(P(D \mid +)\). Redo the problem with counts and check that your four groups add up to the total.

In practice

Quote the base rate with any test result. Sensitivity and specificity are usually quoted as properties of the test, while the base rate differs from clinic to clinic. The chance that a flagged patient is sick differs with it. A common mistake is to use the base rate of a test set that was balanced for training as if it described the clinic.

Where this is used

Used in: precision, recall and screening in A4, the clinic case in F1, and the diabetes screening project (project page). There the base rate of diabetes in one population need not match another.

More questions

A test is 99% sensitive and 99% specific. One patient in 1,000 has the condition. What is the chance that a flagged patient has it?

Sick and flagged: \(0.001\times0.99 = 0.00099\). Healthy and flagged: \(0.999\times0.01 = 0.00999\). The chance is \(0.00099/0.01098 = 9\%\).

Softmax and temperature

Guess first. A classifier gives a photo the scores 2, 1 and −1 for three species. Scores can be negative, but probabilities cannot, and the probabilities must add up to 1. How would you turn the scores into probabilities?

A classifier is a model that sorts inputs into classes, here species. Its score \(z_k\) for class \(k\), also called a logit, is the raw number it gives that class before any probabilities. Softmax computes \(e^{z_k}\), where \(e \approx 2.718\) is the constant used with exponents and logarithms, for the scores of all classes and divides these numbers by their total. The results are positive and add up to 1, so they form a probability distribution. The temperature \(T\) divides the scores first: a low \(T\) gives the highest-scoring class most of the probability, and a high \(T\) spreads it more evenly.

  1. The bars are the softmax probabilities of five made-up scores for one photo. Drag the temperature \(T\) from 1 to 0.3 and the top bar grows from 65.5% to 98.0%. Drag it to 5 and all five bars lie between 12.4% and 28.8%.
  2. Click a species: the boxes under the bars compute \(z/T\), then \(e^{z/T}\), then divide by the total over the five species.
  3. Press “Draw 100” to pick 100 species at random with these probabilities: the dashed outline of a bar is the share of draws that species received, which is near the bar.

At T = 1 the top species gets 65.5%, at T = 0.3 it gets 98.0%, and at T = 5 all five get between 12.4% and 28.8%.

How it works

Take the scores 2, 1 and −1 of the guess. The exponentials are \(e^2\) = 7.389, \(e^1\) = 2.718 and \(e^{-1}\) = 0.368, and they add up to 10.475. The probabilities are 7.389/10.475 = 0.705, 2.718/10.475 = 0.259 and 0.368/10.475 = 0.035.

7.389ez/T for z = 2, T = 1÷10.475total of ez/T over the three classes=0.705softmax probability of that class

The exponential \(e^{z}\) is positive even for a negative score, so all the results are positive, and dividing by the total makes them add up to 1. Take two classes with scores \(z_a\) and \(z_b\) and probabilities \(p_a\) and \(p_b\). Both have the same total in the denominator, so it cancels from the ratio, which is \(p_a/p_b = e^{z_a/T}/e^{z_b/T} = e^{g/T}\) for the gap \(g = z_a - z_b\) between the scores. With \(g = 1\) and \(T = 1\) the ratio is \(0.705/0.259 \approx 2.72 \approx e^1\), and at \(T = 2\) the same gap gives \(e^{0.5} = 1.65\).

Common belief. A softmax probability of 0.98 means the model is 98% sure it is right.

Why it fails. Softmax always returns numbers that add up to 1, even for a photo of a boat, and a model can give 0.98 to a wrong species.

Better account. Read the outputs as a comparison between the classes. Whether 0.98 matches how often the model is right is checked on examples it was not trained on (see grading models).

Quick quiz

Scores of 3, 3 and 3 go into softmax. What probabilities come out?

One third for all three. Only the differences between scores matter, and here they are all zero.

You sample species with the softmax probabilities and want more varied picks. Should you raise or lower \(T\)?

Raise it. A higher temperature flattens the probabilities, so species with lower scores are picked more often.

Go deeper symbols, score gaps, Python, practice, one more question about 3 min

Reading the figure

The scores never change in this figure. Only \(T\) does. After "Draw 100" the outline shows how often the species came up, and it comes closer to the bar as you draw more. At a low temperature, nearly all draws are the top species. At a high temperature, even Ganges sharks, the least likely choice, appear regularly. Language models use this dial when they pick the next word (D3).

Symbols

\[ \mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf{z})_k = \frac{e^{z_k/T}}{\sum_{j} e^{z_j/T}} \]

  • \(z_k\) is the score of class \(k\), and \(\sum_j\) adds over all classes.
  • \(T\) is the temperature. \(T = 1\) is plain softmax. As \(T \to 0\) a class with the largest score (if one score is the largest) gets probability near 1, and as \(T\) grows all classes approach \(1/\text{(number of classes)}\).
  • Adding the same number to all scores leaves the probabilities unchanged, because \(e^{c}\) cancels in the fraction. Only differences between scores matter.

Score gaps and the temperature

A gap of 1 between two scores makes one class 2.7 times as likely as the other, and a gap of 2 makes it 7.4 times as likely. At \(T=2\) the scores of the guess become 1, 0.5 and \(-0.5\), the exponentials 2.718, 1.649 and 0.607, their total 4.974, and the probabilities 0.547, 0.331 and 0.122.

In Python

import numpy as np

z = np.array([2.4, 1.2, 0.5, -0.4, -1.8])   # spadenose, milk, grey bamboo, hammerhead, Ganges

def softmax(z, T=1.0):
    e = np.exp((z - z.max()) / T)           # subtract the largest score: same answer, no overflow
    return e / e.sum()

for T in [0.3, 1.0, 5.0]:
    print(f"T = {T}:", softmax(z, T).round(3))

big = np.array([1000.0, 999.0])
with np.errstate(all="ignore"):
    print("naive :", np.exp(big) / np.exp(big).sum())
print("stable:", softmax(big).round(3))
T = 0.3: [0.98  0.018 0.002 0.    0.   ]
T = 1.0: [0.655 0.197 0.098 0.04  0.01 ]
T = 5.0: [0.288 0.226 0.197 0.164 0.124]
naive : [nan nan]
stable: [0.731 0.269]

z = np.array([2.0, 1.0, -1.0])
e = np.exp(z)
print(e.round(3), e.sum().round(3))
print((e / e.sum()).round(3))
print("ratio of the top two:", round(e[0] / e[1], 3), " e =", round(np.e, 3))
e2 = np.exp(z / 2)
print("T = 2:", (e2 / e2.sum()).round(3))

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Computing \(e^{z}\) for a large score overflows and returns nan. Subtract the largest score first: the probabilities are identical and no number gets large. Softmax functions in the common deep-learning libraries do this.

In practice

Chat tools and APIs offer temperature as a setting. Values below 1 make the output steadier, and a value near 0 picks the top choice almost always. For training, the cross-entropy function of many frameworks, such as PyTorch, takes the raw scores and applies softmax itself (B3).

Where this is used

Used in: the softmax classifier (A3), next-word probabilities and temperature (D3), and attention weights (D4).

More questions

Two classes have scores 0 and \(\ln 3\) (about 1.1). What probabilities does softmax give?

\(e^0 = 1\) and \(e^{\ln 3} = 3\), so the probabilities are \(1/4\) and \(3/4\). A gap of \(\ln 3\) makes one class three times as likely.

Log probability and cross-entropy

Guess first. A model gives the true species the probability 0.9 on one photo, 0.5 on another and 0.01 on a third. For the third photo, would you assign a loss of about 1 (the straight line \(1-p\)), about 5 or about 100?

A loss is a number that is lower when the model does better. The cross-entropy loss of one example is \(\ell = -\ln p\), where \(p\) is the probability that the model gave the true answer and \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm. The loss \(L\) of a data set is the average of \(\ell\) over its \(m\) examples. Because \(\ln p\) is at most 0 and very negative for small \(p\), \(\ell\) is small near \(p = 1\) and climbs steeply as \(p\) falls towards 0.

  1. The right plot shows the loss \(-\ln p\), with a coral dot at the true species' probability \(p\), and the true species is Milk, a milk shark. Slide “Score the model gives the true species” (a made-up raw number before softmax) to 4.8, 2.6 and −2.0, and the box under the plots shows \(p\) = 0.900, 0.499 and 0.010, close to the three photos of the guess, with the loss 0.105, 0.695 and 4.613.
  2. Press “Make it confidently wrong” and \(p\) falls to about 0.001 while the loss rises to 6.605.
True species

The loss rises by 0.59 as p falls from 0.9 to 0.5 but by 2.30 as p falls from 0.1 to 0.01, and it has no upper limit.

How it works

Take the three photos of the guess. The losses are \(-\ln 0.9\) = 0.105, \(-\ln 0.5\) = 0.693 and \(-\ln 0.01\) = 4.605, whereas the straight line \(1-p\) would assign 0.1, 0.5 and 0.99. The three losses add up to 5.40, an average of 1.80, and the third photo supplies 4.605 of the total, which is 85%.

0.105 + 0.693 + 4.605 = 5.40sum of −ln p over the photos÷3m, the number of photos=1.80L, the average loss

One reason for the logarithm is practical. Suppose the examples are independent (one example gives no information about another). Then the probability that a model gives to all its training examples is the product of their probabilities. A product of hundreds of probabilities can be too small for a computer to store, but since \(\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b\), its log is a sum of normal size.

Common belief. Cross-entropy is a complicated way to count mistakes, and accuracy would do.

Why it fails. Model C gives the true species 0.95, 0.95, 0.95 and 0.01 on four photos, and model D gives 0.60, 0.60, 0.60 and 0.30. If a photo counts as right when the true species gets more than 0.5, both have accuracy 0.75, yet their losses are 1.19 and 0.684.

Better account. Accuracy counts right and wrong. Cross-entropy grades the probabilities: it rewards a well-judged doubt and punishes a confident mistake.

Quick quiz

What is the loss when a model gives the true class the probability 0.25?

\(-\ln 0.25 = \ln 4 = 1.386\). It is the loss of a model that spreads its probability evenly over four classes.

Why does a product of probabilities become a sum of logs, and why does that help?

\(\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b\). A sum of a few hundred terms is a normal-sized number, while the product of a few hundred probabilities can be too small for a computer to store.

Go deeper symbols, the slope, accuracy, Python, more questions about 4 min

Reading the figure

You can also pick another true species. The bars show the softmax probabilities of the section above, and the dot shows where the loss lies on the \(-\ln p\) curve. The right-hand curve answers the guess: the straight line \(1-p\) would charge at most 1 for a confident wrong answer, while \(-\ln p\) charges 4.6 at \(p = 0.01\) and keeps climbing. Accuracy only notes that the top pick changed. Cross-entropy also reacts to a model whose top pick is right with a probability of only 0.34 instead of 0.90.

Symbols

\[ \ell = -\ln p_{\text{true}} \qquad L = -\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} \ln p^{(i)}_{\text{true}} \qquad \text{perplexity} = e^{L} \]

  • \(p_{\text{true}}\) is the probability the model gave the correct class, usually from a softmax. \(\ell\) is the loss on one example and \(L\) the average over a batch or data set. Another name for \(-\ln p\) is the surprise of the true answer.
  • If all \(K\) classes get equal probability, \(p = 1/K\) and \(\ell = \ln K\). With five species that is 1.609, the loss to expect at the start of training when the model's scores begin near equal (B8).
  • The slope of \(-\ln p\) with respect to \(p\) is \(-1/p\) (0.6), which grows without limit as \(p\) falls to 0. With softmax the slope with respect to the score of the true class is \(p-1\), which stays between \(-1\) and 0 (see the next part).

The slope with softmax

With softmax, the push on a score is simple. For the true class \(t\), the loss is \(-\ln p_t = -z_t + \ln\sum_j e^{z_j}\). The slope with respect to \(z_k\) is \(-1\) for \(k=t\) and 0 otherwise, from the first term, plus \(e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j} = p_k\) from the second. So the slope is \(p_k - y_k\), where \(y_k\) is 1 for the true class and 0 for the others. For the five scores of the last section with a milk shark as the truth, the slopes are 0.655, \(-0.803\), 0.098, 0.040 and 0.010. The milk score is pushed up with strength 0.80 and the others are pushed down in proportion to their probability. The code checks this by nudging.

Why not accuracy

Accuracy changes in jumps as the parameters of a model change, so its slope is 0 at nearly all points and it cannot tell training which way to move. Cross-entropy changes smoothly with the probabilities, so it has a slope at all points. It also charges a confident mistake heavily by design: in the three-photo example the third photo supplies 85% of the total.

In Python

import numpy as np

# probability each model gave the true species, on four photos
C = np.array([0.95, 0.95, 0.95, 0.01])      # sure of itself, and badly wrong once
D = np.array([0.60, 0.60, 0.60, 0.30])      # careful

for name, p in [("C", C), ("D", D)]:
    print(name, "accuracy", (p > 0.5).mean(), " cross-entropy", round(-np.log(p).mean(), 3))

print("five equal scores:", round(-np.log(1 / 5), 3), "= ln 5 =", round(np.log(5), 3))
C accuracy 0.75  cross-entropy 1.19
D accuracy 0.75  cross-entropy 0.684
five equal scores: 1.609 = ln 5 = 1.609
import numpy as np

# scores for spadenose, milk, grey bamboo, hammerhead, Ganges
z = np.array([2.4, 1.2, 0.5, -0.4, -1.8])
true = 1                         # the photo shows a milk shark

def loss(z):
    p = np.exp(z - z.max())
    p = p / p.sum()
    return -np.log(p[true])

p = np.exp(z) / np.exp(z).sum()
print("p - y   :", (p - np.eye(5)[true]).round(4))
h = 1e-6
nudged = [(loss(z + h * np.eye(5)[k]) - loss(z - h * np.eye(5)[k])) / (2 * h)
          for k in range(5)]
print("nudging :", np.round(nudged, 4))

p3 = np.array([0.9, 0.5, 0.01])    # the three photos of the guess
print(np.round(-np.log(p3), 3), round(-np.log(p3).mean(), 3))

Common mistakes

Debug tip. A probability of 0 gives \(-\ln 0 = \infty\). Libraries compute the loss from the scores directly, or clip \(p\) to a tiny positive number. If your loss turns to inf or nan, check for a zero probability first.

In practice

Many frameworks offer one function that takes raw scores and does softmax and cross-entropy together, using the slope above and avoiding \(\ln 0\). Passing it probabilities applies softmax twice. That common mistake trains slowly and gives losses that look wrong.

Where this is used

Used in: logistic regression and the softmax classifier (A3), the loss for networks (B3), and next-word prediction and perplexity (D3).

More questions

A model's loss on one photo is 0.693. What probability did it give the true class?

\(e^{-0.693} = 0.5\). A loss of \(\ln 2\) means the true class got one half.

Running averages

Guess first. Daily water temperature readings vary by about half a degree. You want a steady estimate that still follows the change when the monsoon cools the sea. Would you average all readings so far, only the last 5, or something else?

The running mean is the mean of all readings so far, so it weights an old reading as much as a new one. An exponential moving average (EMA) instead forms a new average from the share \(\beta\) of the old average and the share \(1-\beta\) of the new reading. Here the decay \(\beta\) is a number between 0 and 1. A decay near 1 smooths the readings strongly and responds slowly, and a decay near 0 smooths little and responds quickly.

  1. The dots are made-up daily temperatures, the sand line is the running mean and the coral line is the EMA with \(\beta\) = 0.9. After the sea cools on day 60, the EMA is at 26.90 °C on day 80 (box under the plots) while the running mean is still near 28 °C.
  2. Drag \(\beta\) to 0.99: the coral line is smoother, but on day 80 it is still at 27.82 °C. Drag \(\beta\) to 0 and the EMA equals the reading of the day.

After the sea cools on day 60, the EMA with β = 0.9 is at 26.9 °C by day 80, while the running mean is still near 28 °C.

How it works

Take day 80 with \(\beta\) = 0.9. The average of day 79 is 26.80 °C and the reading of day 80 is 27.86 °C, so the new average is \(0.9\times26.80 + 0.1\times27.86\), about 26.9 °C.

0.9β, the share of the old average×26.80average on day 79, °C+0.11 − β, the share of the new reading×27.86reading on day 80, °C=26.9average on day 80, °C

A new day multiplies the weight of all older readings by \(\beta\), so a reading \(k\) days old has the weight \((1-\beta)\beta^k\). As an approximation, a reading \(1/(1-\beta)\) days old keeps about a third of today's weight. So the EMA behaves roughly like an average of that many recent readings, 10 for \(\beta\) = 0.9 and 100 for \(\beta\) = 0.99. If the readings stay at a new level, the part of the old gap that is left after \(k\) days is \(\beta^k\). So the EMA has closed the share \(1-\beta^k\). For \(\beta\) = 0.9 that is 65% after 10 days and 90% after 22 days, and for \(\beta\) = 0.99 the 90% mark takes about 229 days.

Common belief. To get a steady estimate, average all the readings so far.

Why it fails. After day 60 the running mean still includes the 60 warm days. On day 120 it is near 27.5 °C, while the readings since day 60 average about 26.6 °C.

Better account. Weight recent readings more. The decay \(\beta\) sets how fast old readings fade, and a larger \(\beta\) smooths more but responds later.

Quick quiz

With \(\beta = 0.99\), about how many recent readings does the EMA effectively average?

About \(1/(1-0.99) = 100\), as an approximation.

With \(\beta = 0.5\), what weights do today's and yesterday's readings get?

Today's reading gets \(1-\beta = 0.5\) and yesterday's gets \(0.5\times0.5 = 0.25\). The weights halve from one day to the next, and the average forgets quickly.

Go deeper symbols, starting at 0, bucket analogy, Python about 3 min

Reading the figure

The lower plot shows the weights: a reading \(k\) days old counts \((1-\beta)\beta^k\), which shrinks by the same factor per day. Slide \(\beta\) towards 0 and the coral line follows the readings closely, and slide it towards 0.99 and it becomes smooth and slow. The weights add up to 1 once many days have passed, and the effective window of about \(1/(1-\beta)\) days is a rule of thumb.

Symbols

\[ \bar{x}_t = \beta\,\bar{x}_{t-1} + (1-\beta)\,x_t \qquad \bar{x}_t = (1-\beta)\sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\beta^{k}\,x_{t-k} \]

  • \(x_t\) is the reading on day \(t\) and \(\bar{x}_t\) the moving average after day \(t\). \(\beta\) is the decay.
  • The second form shows that the EMA is a weighted mean of all past readings, with weights \((1-\beta)\beta^k\) for a reading \(k\) days old.
  • Momentum and Adam (B5) use this update on gradients, with \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\).

Starting at 0

By hand with \(\beta=0.9\), starting from 0. After the first reading, \(\bar{x}_1 = 0.9\times0 + 0.1\times28.4 = 2.84\). After the second, \(\bar{x}_2 = 0.9\times2.84 + 0.1\times28.9 = 2.556 + 2.89 = 5.446\). Dividing by \(1-\beta^t\) repairs the start: \(2.84/0.1 = 28.4\) and \(5.446/0.19 = 28.66\). The weights on today's reading and the two before it are 0.1, 0.09 and 0.081.

An analogy: a leaky bucket

Analogy. A leaky bucket. Day by day you pour in a small share of today's water, and a share of the old water leaks out.

Where it breaks. A bucket that leaks a fixed amount per day forgets old water completely. An EMA never does: its weights shrink but never reach zero. A moving average of the last \(N\) readings, by contrast, drops a reading entirely on day \(N+1\).

In Python

import numpy as np

x = np.array([28.4, 28.9, 27.8, 28.6, 29.1, 28.2, 28.5, 28.7])   # daily water temperature, made-up
beta = 0.9

m, raw, fixed = 0.0, [], []
for t, value in enumerate(x, start=1):
    m = beta * m + (1 - beta) * value       # start the average at 0
    raw.append(m)
    fixed.append(m / (1 - beta ** t))       # divide out the pull towards 0

print("start at 0   :", np.round(raw, 2))
print("bias-corrected:", np.round(fixed, 2))
print("plain mean    :", round(x.mean(), 2))
start at 0   : [ 2.84  5.45  7.68  9.77 11.71 13.36 14.87 16.25]
bias-corrected: [28.4  28.66 28.34 28.42 28.59 28.5  28.5  28.54]
plain mean    : 28.52
import numpy as np

# weights on the last three readings, and days to close 90% of a jump
for beta in [0.9, 0.99]:
    days = np.log(0.1) / np.log(beta)
    weights = [round((1 - beta) * beta ** k, 4) for k in range(3)]
    print(f"beta = {beta}: weights {weights}, 90% of a jump after {days:.0f} days")
beta = 0.9: weights [0.1, 0.09, 0.081], 90% of a jump after 22 days
beta = 0.99: weights [0.01, 0.0099, 0.0098], 90% of a jump after 229 days

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If you start an EMA at 0, its first values are biased towards 0. Choose the "Start at 0" option in the figure to see this. Adam divides by \(1-\beta^t\) to fix this, which is why that factor appears in B5.

In practice

Adam's usual settings are \(\beta_1 = 0.9\) for the average of gradients and \(\beta_2 = 0.999\) for the average of squared gradients (Kingma and Ba, 2015). A batch norm layer in PyTorch blends 10% of the newest batch into its running mean by default, which is \(\beta = 0.9\) (B6).

Where this is used

Used in: momentum and Adam (B5), smoothing a noisy training-loss curve (B8), and the running averages inside batch norm (B6).

More questions

Why does an EMA started at 0 read too low at first?

The first updates keep a share \(\beta\) of the starting 0, so the average is dragged towards 0 until enough readings have been mixed in.

Expectation and sampling noise

Guess first. SharkCam, the book's underwater camera, sees 0, 1, 2 or 3 sharks on a dive (made-up counts), and the long-run average is 0.75. After 10 dives the average could be 0.4, 0.75 or 1.2. After 1,000 dives, how close do you expect it to be?

The expectation \(E[X]\) of a count \(X\) is its long-run average, the sum of the outcomes multiplied by their probabilities. The average of \(n\) independent dives (the result of one dive gives no information about another) differs from 0.75 by sampling noise, whose typical size is the standard error \(\mathrm{SE} = \sigma/\sqrt{n}\). Here \(\sigma\) is the SD of one dive's count. Four times as many dives halve the standard error.

  1. The eight lines are simulated runs: the average number of sharks per dive after 1, 2, 3 and more dives. The solid line is the expectation 0.75, and the dotted funnel marks where about 95% of averages fall. Drag “Number of dives” to 10 and then to 1,000: the box under the plot gives the funnel as 0.75 ± 0.550 and then 0.75 ± 0.055.
  2. Press “New runs”: the lines change, but at 1,000 dives most of them again lie inside the funnel.

After 10 dives about 95% of the averages lie within ±0.55 of 0.75, and after 1,000 dives within ±0.055.

How it works

Add up outcomes times probabilities. The made-up dive counts 0, 1, 2 and 3 have the probabilities 0.50, 0.30, 0.15 and 0.05, so their expectation is below.

0 × 0.50no sharks, half the dives+1 × 0.301 shark+2 × 0.152 sharks+3 × 0.053 sharks=0.75E[X], sharks per dive

Then find the standard error. The squared deviations of the counts 0, 1, 2 and 3 from 0.75 are 0.5625, 0.0625, 1.5625 and 5.0625. Their average weighted by the probabilities is the variance of one dive's count, \(0.5\times0.5625 + 0.3\times0.0625 + 0.15\times1.5625 + 0.05\times5.0625 = 0.7875\), so \(\sigma\) = 0.887. For \(n\) = 10 dives \(\mathrm{SE} = 0.887/\sqrt{10} = 0.28\). The average of many dives is close to a normal curve, and 1.96 SDs contain 95% of a normal curve, so about 95% of averages lie within \(1.96\times0.28 = 0.55\) of 0.75. The \(\sqrt{n}\) arises because the variance of a sum of independent cases is the sum of their variances, \(n\sigma^2\). Dividing the sum by \(n\) divides all deviations by \(n\), and the variance squares deviations, so the average has variance \(n\sigma^2/n^2 = \sigma^2/n\) and SD \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\).

Common belief. A model's test score is a fixed property of the model.

Why it fails. The score is an average over one test set, so another test set of the same size would give a different score, by about \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) when the cases are independent. Here \(n\) is the number of cases and \(\sigma\) is the SD of the result (right or wrong) on one case.

Better account. A score is an estimate with noise, so report the size of the test set and the standard error. Also check that the cases are independent (neighbouring video frames are not).

Quick quiz

A test set has 100 frames and the score varies by about 4 percentage points from set to set. How many frames would bring that to about 2 points?

You would need 400. The standard error goes with \(1/\sqrt{n}\), so halving it needs four times the frames.

What is the expectation of one roll of a fair six-sided die?

\((1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5\). The expectation need not be a value the die can show.

Go deeper symbols, a shortcut, correlated frames, Python, more about 3 min

Reading the figure

Early averages vary widely because a single dive makes up a large share of the average, and later averages stay close to the expectation. The lines differ from run to run, and no single run is special. The funnel narrows like \(1/\sqrt{n}\), which is slow: to halve the noise you need four times the data. The same arithmetic applies to a model's test score, which is an average of right-or-wrong results over the test set, when the cases are independent.

Symbols

\[ E[X] = \sum_k p_k\,x_k \qquad \mathrm{SE} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \]

  • \(p_k\) is the probability of outcome \(x_k\). The sum runs over all outcomes.
  • \(\sigma\) is the SD of one case, here \(\sqrt{0.7875} = 0.887\) sharks. SE is the standard error, and about 95% of averages fall within 1.96 SE of the expectation.

A shortcut for the variance

The numbers behind the funnel. First \(E[X^2] = 0\times0.5 + 1\times0.3 + 4\times0.15 + 9\times0.05 = 1.35\). The variance is \(1.35 - 0.75^2 = 0.7875\) and the SD is 0.887. Then \(\mathrm{SE} = 0.887/\sqrt{10} = 0.28\) for 10 dives, so 95% of averages fall within \(1.96\times0.28 = 0.55\) of 0.75. For 1,000 dives the SE is 0.028 and the range is 0.055.

When the cases are not independent

The formula needs independent cases. The 2,400 frames of the made-up dive log come from one dive at one frame per second, and neighbouring frames are likely to look nearly alike. They count as far fewer than 2,400 independent cases, so the true noise of a score on them is larger than \(\sigma/\sqrt{2400}\) says.

In Python

import numpy as np

values = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3])             # sharks seen on a dive
probs = np.array([0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05])
print("expectation:", (values * probs).sum())

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
dives = rng.choice(values, size=1000, p=probs)
for n in [10, 100, 1000]:
    print(f"average after {n:4d} dives:", dives[:n].mean())

sigma = np.sqrt((probs * values**2).sum() - 0.75**2)
print("standard error at n = 100:", round(sigma / np.sqrt(100), 3))
expectation: 0.75
average after   10 dives: 1.0
average after  100 dives: 0.91
average after 1000 dives: 0.787
standard error at n = 100: 0.089

In this run, the first 10 dives gave 1.0, a gap of 0.25. That is within the standard error of 0.28 for 10 dives. With another seed, the average could fall anywhere in the funnel.

import numpy as np

p = 0.82                      # share of test frames a model gets right
for n in [200, 2000]:
    se = np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
    print(f"n = {n}: standard error {se:.4f},",
          f"95% range +/- {1.96 * se * 100:.1f} points")
n = 200: standard error 0.0272, 95% range +/- 5.3 points
n = 2000: standard error 0.0086, 95% range +/- 1.7 points

In practice

For a rare class the useful test size is the number of cases of that class. Three Ganges records can give a recall of only 0, 1/3, 2/3 or 1.

Where this is used

Used in: how much to trust a score on a held-out set (A4), batch size and gradient noise (B3), and the next two sections.

More questions

A test set has 3,000 frames cut from five long dives. Why might the noise of the score be larger than \(\sigma/\sqrt{3000}\) suggests?

Frames from one dive are alike, so they act as fewer independent cases. The formula counts 3,000 independent cases and overstates the evidence.

Confidence intervals and the bootstrap

Guess first. A model from my diabetes screening project gets 121 of the 154 women in its test set right, which is 78.6%. On a different 154 women, would it score the same? How far could the score differ?

Report a test score with a range, because another test set would give another score. The bootstrap imitates new test sets by resampling. A resample is a draw of as many cases as the test set has, taken from the test set with replacement, so a case can be drawn again. The middle 95% of the scores of many resamples is a 95% confidence interval. The true score is the share the model would get right on all possible cases, and the interval comes from a method meant to contain it in 95 of 100 repeated studies. A formula gives a similar interval without resampling.

  1. The histogram shows 300 resamples (coral line: the observed 78.6%). The teal bars are the middle 95%: 71.4% to 84.4% in the box under the plot, next to the formula's 72.1% to 85.1%.
  2. Press “Run 100 studies” and the lines are the formula's intervals from 100 simulated test sets, drawn with the true score set to 78.6%. The box counts those that contain the true score: 95 at first, usually 90 to 96 later.
  3. Choose “One test set, resampled”, then drag “Number of test women n” to 1,500 at the same 78.6% and the box shows the formula's interval narrowing to 76.5% to 80.7%.

At 78.6% right, the 95% interval is about 72% to 85% for 154 women and about 76.5% to 80.7% for 1,500 women.

How it works

Compute the formula for 121 of 154. The standard error of a share \(\hat{p}\) is \(\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}\). This is the standard error \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) of the previous section, with \(\sigma = \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}\) as the SD of one right-or-wrong result. Here the share right is \(\hat{p}\) = 121/154 = 0.786, so \(\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\) = 0.786 × 0.214 = 0.168. Dividing by \(n\) = 154 gives 0.00109, and the square root, the standard error, is 0.033. Then 1.96 × 0.033 = 0.065, so the interval is 0.786 ± 0.065, from 0.721 to 0.851.

0.786\(\hat{p}\), the share right±1.96SDs that contain 95% of a normal curve×0.033\(\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}\), the standard error=0.721 to 0.851the 95% interval

The factor 1.96 is used because 95% of the area of a normal curve lies within 1.96 SDs of the mean. The formula assumes that the share varies like a normal curve, a poor assumption for few cases (see the fold).

Common belief. A 95% interval means there is a 95% chance that the true value is inside this one.

Why it fails. The true value is a fixed number, and a given interval either contains it or misses it. What varies from study to study is the interval, and the 95% describes the method across repeated studies, as the 100 studies of the figure show.

Better account. Read the 95% as a property of the method, and report the score with its interval and the test size.

Quick quiz

Why does a resample contain 154 women when only 154 women exist?

Women are drawn with replacement, so the same woman can be drawn several times and others not at all. A resample has the same size as the test set, which keeps the noise level right.

Two models both score 80%, one on 100 frames and one on 1,000. Which interval is narrower, and by roughly how much?

The 1,000-frame interval is narrower by a factor of \(\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2\).

Go deeper resampling, what 95% means, symbols, Python, more about 4 min

How the figure resamples

The score 121 of 154 is that of the rebuilt XGBoost model in my diabetes screening project. To see how much it could differ, the bootstrap acts as if the 154 women were the whole population. A resample draws 154 women from them with replacement, so some women appear twice and some not at all, and takes the share of the drawn women that the model got right. Press "Resample 200" to add 200 more resamples to the histogram. The middle 95% of the resampled scores, shown in teal, is the interval. Raise the slider and the interval narrows like \(1/\sqrt{n}\), the same law as in the section on sampling noise.

What 95% means

What does "95%" mean? Switch to "100 repeated studies". The lines are separate studies, with a new test set, a new score and its own interval from the formula. The teal line is the true score, which we know only because this is a simulation: it is set to 78.6%. Most of the 100 intervals cross it, and the rest (coral) miss. At this test size the formula's intervals contain the true score in about 93% of studies (a calculation from the binomial distribution gives 93.4%), a little below the 95% they are built for, so the count varies around 93 from press to press. At 1,500 women the same calculation gives 94.9%. The 95% describes the method across repeated studies. Any single interval either contains the truth or does not. It can be read as the range of true scores that the test result does not rule out at the 5% level.

Symbols

\[ \hat{p} \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}\,(1-\hat{p})}{n}} \]

  • \(\hat{p}\), read "p hat", is the observed share right (here 121/154 = 0.786) and \(n\) the test set size.
  • The square root is the standard error of a share. The 1.96 comes from the normal curve: 95% of the area lies within 1.96 SDs. For 121 of 154 the formula gives 72.1% to 85.1%, close to the bootstrap interval.

The formula for 1,500 women

With 1,500 women the standard error is 0.0106, the margin 0.021, and the interval runs from 0.765 to 0.806.

When the formula breaks

For few cases the formula breaks. If a model finds 2 of the 3 Ganges sharks, \(\hat{p} = 0.67\), and the formula gives 0.13 to 1.20. An upper end above 100% is impossible. The bootstrap interval of three cases runs from 0 to 1. Both results say that three cases tell you very little about recall.

In Python

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
right = np.array([1] * 121 + [0] * 33)      # 121 of 154 held-out women called correctly
print("score:", round(right.mean(), 3))

boot = [rng.choice(right, size=154, replace=True).mean() for _ in range(5000)]
low, high = np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5])
print("95% interval:", round(low, 3), "to", round(high, 3))

p = right.mean()
print("formula     :", round(p - 1.96 * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / 154), 3), "to", round(p + 1.96 * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / 154), 3))
score: 0.786
95% interval: 0.721 to 0.851
formula     : 0.721 to 0.851
import numpy as np

right = np.array([1, 1, 0])          # 2 of the 3 Ganges sharks found
p = right.mean()
se = np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / 3)
print("formula  :", round(p - 1.96 * se, 2), "to", round(p + 1.96 * se, 2))

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
boot = [rng.choice(right, size=3, replace=True).mean() for _ in range(5000)]
print("bootstrap:", np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5]).round(2))
formula  : 0.13 to 1.2
bootstrap: [0. 1.]

Common mistakes

Debug tip. The bootstrap only describes noise from a finite test set. Suppose the test women come from a different population than the people the model will meet, such as Pima women versus Mumbai patients. Then the interval can be narrow and still misleading (C3, F1).

In practice

Write a score with its interval and the test size, such as 78.6% (95% interval 72.1 to 85.1, 154 women). Overlapping intervals are a blunt way to compare two models. Grade both on the same cases and use the paired comparison of the next section.

Where this is used

Used in: reporting a test score (A4), comparing a model with its baseline (A1), and the test in the next section.

More questions

At the same test size, is the interval wider for a score near 50% or near 95%?

Near 50%. The quantity \(\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\) is 0.25 at one half and 0.048 at 0.95, so the standard error is about 2.3 times larger near 50%.

Is model B better than model A?

Guess first. In made-up results, SharkCam's model A gets 82.0% of 200 test frames (video images) right and a new model B gets 85.5%. Is B better, or could this gap come from luck in which frames were chosen?

A paired comparison grades both models on the same frames. Only the frames where just one model is right can separate them, because the other frames add the same to both accuracies. The null hypothesis is that the models do not differ, so such a frame is equally likely to favour A or B, like a coin flip. The p-value is the probability, if the null hypothesis were true, of a split between A and B at least as uneven as the one observed.

  1. The bars give the probability that B wins a given number of the 15 frames of disagreement if they were coin flips. The teal line marks the observed 11, and the coral bars, the splits at least as uneven, add up to the p-value 0.118.
  2. Press “Flip coins in 2,000 imaginary worlds”: the diamonds show the simulated frequencies, which follow the bars.
  3. Set “Frames where only one model is right” to 60 and “Of those, frames won by model B” to 40: the p-value falls to 0.013.

A fair coin gives a split at least as uneven as 11 wins out of 15 about 12% of the time, so luck could explain B's gap.

How it works

Count the 200 frames. Of them, 160 are right for both models and 25 are wrong for both, so these 185 frames cannot favour either. In the other 15, A alone is right on 4 frames and B alone on 11, so A is right on 164 (82.0%) and B on 171 (85.5%).

2both directions: 11 to 4 and 4 to 11×1,365 + 455 + 105 + 15 + 1 = 1,941ways for B to win 11 to 15 of the 15 flips÷215 = 32,768equally likely sequences of 15 flips=0.118the p-value

Here \(\binom{15}{11}\) counts the ways to choose which 11 of the 15 frames B wins. It equals \(15\times14\times13\times12/(4\times3\times2\times1) = 1{,}365\), and the other four numbers count 12 to 15 wins in the same way. The factor 2 adds the equally uneven splits in which A wins 11 or more.

Common belief. A p-value of 0.12 means a 12% chance that the models are equal, so B is 88% likely to be better.

Why it fails. The p-value is computed by assuming that the models are equal. It measures how surprising the data are under that assumption, which differs from the probability that the assumption is true.

Better account. A p-value of 0.12 says that luck alone would produce a split this uneven about 1 time in 8. It does not measure the size or importance of an effect.

Quick quiz

Why do the 160 frames that both models get right play no part in the test?

They do not separate the models. Only a frame where one model is right and the other wrong can favour either one.

B wins 9 of the 10 frames where the models disagree. Is the two-sided p-value below 0.05?

Yes. \(\binom{10}{9} = 10\) and \(\binom{10}{10} = 1\), so \(2\times(10+1)/1024 = 0.021\). With so few disagreements, a split of 9 to 1 is needed. A split of 8 to 2 gives 0.109.

Go deeper symbols, how many wins, a shortcut, Python, more about 4 min

Reading the figure

With 60 frames of disagreement and B winning 40, the p-value is 0.013, so a split this uneven would be rare if the two models were equal. The diamonds are the frequencies you get by simulation, and they follow the calculated bars. Note what the test does not say. It does not say how large B's edge is, or whether the edge is worth the cost of switching. The confidence interval of the last section addresses size.

Symbols

\[ p\text{-value} = 2\sum_{k=b}^{d}\binom{d}{k}\frac{1}{2^{d}} \qquad \text{(for } b \ge d/2\text{)} \]

  • \(d\) is the number of frames where only one model is right and \(b\) the number B wins (the larger of the two counts).
  • \(\binom{d}{k}\) counts the ways \(k\) of \(d\) coin flips can come up heads (0.4). Dividing by \(2^d\) turns the count into a probability, and the 2 adds the equally uneven split in the other direction. This is the sign test, a simple form of McNemar's test.

The statement on p-values

The American Statistical Association's 2016 statement says that a p-value does not measure the size or importance of an effect. It also says that a decision should not rest only on whether a p-value crosses a threshold such as 0.05.

How many wins are enough

How many wins are enough? With 15 disagreements, a split of 12 to 3 gives \(2\times(455+105+15+1)/32{,}768 = 0.035\), under 0.05. A split of 11 to 4 gives 0.118. So B needs 12 wins out of 15 to bring the p-value under 0.05. The same accuracy gap can also count for more or less. B winning 11 to 4 is a net gain of 7 frames with \(p=0.118\). B winning 17 to 10 is also a net gain of 7, over 27 disagreements, and gives \(p=0.248\). More disagreement means more noise around the same net gain.

A shortcut for many disagreements

With many disagreements the bell curve is a good shortcut. Under coin flips the wins of B have mean \(d/2\) and SD \(\sqrt{d}/2\). For 40 of 60, \(z = (39.5-30)/3.87 = 2.45\), where 39.5 includes a half-step correction. The two-sided p-value is 0.014, close to the 0.013 of the full count.

In Python

import numpy as np
from math import comb

d, b = 15, 11                               # 15 frames where the models differ; B won 11
tail = sum(comb(d, k) for k in range(b, d + 1)) / 2 ** d
print("one side :", round(tail, 4))
print("two sides:", round(2 * tail, 4))

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
wins = rng.binomial(d, 0.5, size=100000)    # B's wins if each frame were a coin flip
print("simulated:", np.mean(np.abs(wins - d / 2) >= abs(b - d / 2)))
one side : 0.0592
two sides: 0.1185
simulated: 0.11945
from math import comb, sqrt, erf

def p_value(d, b):
    return 2 * sum(comb(d, k) for k in range(b, d + 1)) / 2 ** d

# with 15 disagreements, 12 wins is enough and 11 is not
print(round(p_value(15, 12), 4), round(p_value(15, 11), 4))
# the same net gain of 7 frames, over 15 and over 27 disagreements
print(round(p_value(15, 11), 3), round(p_value(27, 17), 3))
# bell-curve shortcut for 40 of 60
z = (39.5 - 30) / (sqrt(60) / 2)
normal = 2 * (1 - 0.5 * (1 + erf(z / sqrt(2))))
print(round(p_value(60, 40), 4), round(normal, 4))
0.0352 0.1185
0.118 0.248
0.0135 0.0142

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Try 20 models and pick the best, and by luck alone the best is likely to look better than A: if all 20 models, none better than A, independently had a 5% chance of reaching \(p < 0.05\) by luck, the chance that at least one does is \(1-0.95^{20} = 64\%\). Decide on the test and the test set before looking, and confirm the winner on a fresh set (A4).

In practice

The test needs disagreements. Two models that are nearly identical produce few of them, and then no test set of a sensible size can separate them. Libraries offer this paired test as McNemar's test.

Where this is used

Used in: comparing models and settings fairly (A4, A6), and judging whether an adaptation method helps (C3).

More questions

A p-value is 0.03. Does that prove B is much better?

No. It says luck alone rarely gives a split this uneven. B's edge could still be tiny, and with enough frames even a tiny edge gives a small p-value.

Correlation and causation

Guess first. On warm days, ice-cream sales at Juhu beach go up, and so do shark sightings. A local politician proposes banning ice-cream sales to cut sightings. Would it work?

The correlation \(r\) of two columns is a number from −1 to 1 for how closely their points lie along a straight line. It is near 1 for a rising line, near −1 for a falling line and near 0 for neither. Two columns can be correlated because a third quantity, a confounder, drives both. Causation means that changing one thing would change the other, and an intervention tests it: setting one of them by hand instead of watching it vary.

  1. A dot is a day (made up): cones sold across, sightings up, and the colour shows the water temperature, navy for cool and coral for warm. The 150 days form a cloud that slopes upward, and the box under the plot gives \(r\) = 0.89.
  2. Press “Look at one temperature only” and the window of water temperatures narrows to 27 ± 0.4 °C, only 11 days stay in full colour (the other dots fade), and \(r\) falls to −0.10.
  3. Choose “Ban ice cream”: all dots move to 0 cones, and the average sightings stay at 2.10.

Over 150 made-up days \(r\) = 0.89, within ±0.4 °C of 27 °C it is −0.10, and banning ice cream leaves sightings unchanged.

How it works

Take five made-up days with water temperatures 27, 28, 29, 30 and 31 °C and sightings 2, 1, 4, 3 and 5. The temperatures have mean 29 and SD 1.41, so their z-scores (see the normal curve) are −1.41, −0.71, 0, 0.71 and 1.41. With mean 3 and SD 1.41, the sightings have the z-scores −0.71, −1.41, 0.71, 0 and 1.41. The correlation \(r\) is the mean of the products of the paired z-scores, and multiplying the pairs gives 1, 1, 0, 0 and 2, so \(r\) = 0.8.

1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 4sum of the products of z-scores÷5n, the number of days=0.8r, the correlation

A product of two z-scores is positive when both values lie on the same side of their means, so \(r\) is positive when the columns rise together. The made-up days were generated so that ice-cream sales and sightings both depend on the water temperature and not on one another. That is why \(r\) = 0.89 over all days, why it is near 0 among days of similar temperature, and why banning ice cream moves only the cones.

Common belief. If two things move together, one causes the other.

Why it fails. A third quantity may drive both (a confounder, as here), the second thing may drive the first, or a small sample may produce a pattern by chance.

Better account. Set one of them by hand, which is an experiment, or compare cases that match on a confounder you have measured, as the narrow window does.

Quick quiz

Hospitals with more doctors have more deaths. Name a confounder.

Hospital size, or how ill the patients are. Large hospitals treat more and sicker patients, which raises both the number of doctors and the number of deaths.

Two columns have \(r = 0\). Does that mean they are unrelated?

No. \(r\) measures straight-line trends only. If \(y = x^2\) for \(x\) from \(-2\) to 2, then \(r=0\) while \(y\) depends fully on \(x\).

Go deeper symbols, straight lines and sample size, Python, more about 4 min

Reading the figure

Warm days (coral) appear up and to the right, cool days (navy) down and to the left, so the cloud slopes upward. Once the window contains only days with nearly the same temperature, the slope disappears: with the water held fixed, ice-cream sales say little about sightings. When you press "Ban ice cream", the dots move to zero sales and the sightings do not change, because these made-up sightings were generated from the water temperature alone. The diagram at the top shows that structure: temperature drives both, and no arrow runs between them. (In small windows, with only a dozen days, \(r\) varies by chance, as the section on sampling noise explains.)

Computing r

The correlation \(r\) can be computed with the tool from the normal-curve section: standardise both columns, multiply the z-scores day by day and average the products. It is +1 when the points lie on a rising line and −1 on a falling line.

Symbols

\[ r = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} z_x^{(i)}\, z_y^{(i)} \]

  • \(z_x^{(i)}\) and \(z_y^{(i)}\) are the z-scores of day \(i\) for the two columns, and \(n\) the number of days.
  • Written as vectors of z-scores, \(r = \mathbf{z}_x\cdot\mathbf{z}_y / n\): a dot product (0.5) that equals the cosine of the angle between them.

Straight lines and sample size

Correlation sees only straight-line trends. If \(x\) runs from \(-2\) to 2 and \(y = x^2\), then \(y\) is fixed by \(x\) and still \(r=0\), because the left side falls while the right side rises. Correlation also needs enough days. As a rough rule, \(r\) can be told apart from zero at the 5% level only if its size exceeds about \(1.96/\sqrt{n}\), which is 0.16 for 150 days and 0.57 for 12 days. That is why \(r\) varies widely in the narrow windows of the figure.

Correlations in models

Fitted models can pick up correlations that are not causes: a shark detector may pick up "blue water" instead of sharks (B9).

In Python

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
temp = rng.uniform(25, 30, size=200)                          # water temperature, made-up days
ice = 55 + 20 * (temp - 27) + rng.normal(0, 9, size=200)      # cones sold
seen = 2 + 1.1 * (temp - 27) + rng.normal(0, 0.9, size=200)   # shark sightings

print("r over all days:", round(np.corrcoef(ice, seen)[0, 1], 2))
band = np.abs(temp - 27) < 0.4                                # days with nearly the same temperature
print("days in band   :", band.sum())
print("r inside band  :", round(np.corrcoef(ice[band], seen[band])[0, 1], 2))
r over all days: 0.83
days in band   : 31
r inside band  : 0.1

The code draws its own made-up days, so its numbers differ a little from the figure's.

import numpy as np

temp = np.array([27, 28, 29, 30, 31.0])           # five made-up days
seen = np.array([2, 1, 4, 3, 5.0])
z = lambda a: (a - a.mean()) / a.std()
print("z of temperature:", z(temp).round(2))
print("z of sightings  :", z(seen).round(2))
r_own = (z(temp) * z(seen)).mean()
print("r =", round(r_own, 2), " numpy:", round(np.corrcoef(temp, seen)[0, 1], 2))

x = np.arange(-2.0, 3.0)
print("y = x**2, fully set by x:", round(abs(np.corrcoef(x, x ** 2)[0, 1]), 2))
for n in [150, 12]:
    print(n, "days: |r| must beat about", round(1.96 / np.sqrt(n), 2))
z of temperature: [-1.41 -0.71  0.    0.71  1.41]
z of sightings  : [-0.71 -1.41  0.71  0.    1.41]
r = 0.8  numpy: 0.8
y = x**2, fully set by x: 0.0
150 days: |r| must beat about 0.16
12 days: |r| must beat about 0.57

Common mistakes

Debug tip. One \(r\) for a pooled data set can mislead. Mixing two groups can create a correlation that neither group has, or hide one that both have. Colour the points by group before trusting a single number.

In practice

Plot two columns before you quote a correlation. Look for groups, outliers and the sample size. A strong link between a feature and a label can be a shortcut, such as water colour read as a sign of sharks (B9).

Where this is used

Used in: feature importance and its limits (A6), spurious cues in images (B9), and subgroup checks in health data (F1).

More questions

How would you test whether ice cream affects sightings?

Intervene: set sales high on some days and low on others at random, with the water temperature varying freely, and compare sightings. Or compare days of nearly equal temperature, as the figure does.

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory For the values 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9, find the mean, variance and SD (divide by \(n\)). Then add 10 to all values, and then multiply the original values by 3. How do the mean and SD change in these cases? Finally standardise the original values and check that the result has mean 0 and SD 1.

    Hint

    The mean of the original values is 5. Work out the deviations first.

  2. theory A screening test has 95% sensitivity and 98% specificity. In 10,000 patients, 2% have the condition. Fill in the four counts and find the chance that a flagged patient has it. Then suppose flagged patients get a second, independent test of the same quality and flagged again. What is the chance now?

  3. theory Compute the softmax of the scores \((2, 0, -2)\) at \(T = 1\). Show that adding 5 to all scores leaves the probabilities unchanged. What happens to the probabilities as \(T \to 0\), and as \(T \to \infty\)?

  4. theory An EMA has \(\beta = 0.8\). Give the weight on the reading from today, 1 day ago and 2 days ago. What is the effective window? Show that the weights \((1-\beta)\beta^k\) add up to 1, using the sum of a geometric series.

    Hint

    \(1 + \beta + \beta^2 + \dots = 1/(1-\beta)\) for \(0 \le \beta < 1\).

Practice

  1. practice Load the catch records (../data/sharks/catch.csv, 600 made-up sharks) with pandas. Standardise length_cm over all sharks and list the five largest z-scores with their species. Then standardise separately for the species and compare the largest z-scores. Which version flags a shark that is unusual for its own species?

  2. practice Take the 200 milk sharks in the catch records and find the share that are mature. Build a 95% bootstrap interval for it with 5,000 resamples, and compare it with the formula \(\hat{p} \pm 1.96\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}\).

  3. practice Two models are scored on 12 frames, 1 for right and 0 for wrong. A: [1,1,0,1,0,1,1,0,1,1,0,1]. B: [1,1,1,1,1,1,0,1,1,1,0,1]. Find the frames where they differ, how many B wins, and the two-sided p-value. What does the answer say about the evidence from 12 frames?

  4. practice Write an EMA with bias correction and run it on x = 28 + 0.5 * np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=100) with the last 50 values lowered by 2. For \(\beta = 0.5, 0.9, 0.99\), find the first day after the drop on which the EMA is within 0.5 of the new level. Report "never" if it does not happen in the 50 days. Compare with \(1/(1-\beta)\).

Think deeper

  1. open The clinic wants to screen all its patients with a test that has 90% sensitivity and 90% specificity. Nobody knows the base rate for its patients. What would you want to find out first, how would the answer change your plan, and what harms follow from false alarms in a screening programme?

  2. open Model B beats model A by 1.5 points on 200 frames, and switching costs a week of work. What would you measure and test before switching? Think about the size of the test set and the kinds of mistakes. Think about the cost of the two kinds (missing a Ganges shark versus a false alarm) and the water conditions the model will meet.

  3. open A newspaper says: "Ice-cream sales and shark sightings rise together, so ban ice cream." Write a reply of five sentences using the tools of this chapter. Then say what data would convince you that some factor does cause more sightings.

Come back later

Try these after two days and again after a week. Answer first, then open.

The loss is \(-\ln p\) and its slope is \(-1/p\) (0.6). Use the slope to estimate how much the loss falls when \(p\) rises from 0.50 to 0.51, then compare with the true change.

The slope at 0.5 is \(-2\), so a rise of 0.01 lowers the loss by about 0.02. The true change is \(\ln 0.51 - \ln 0.50 = 0.0198\) lower. The slope gives a close estimate for a small nudge.

The correlation is \(r = \mathbf{z}_x\cdot\mathbf{z}_y/n\). What is the length of a z-score vector, and what does \(r\) equal in terms of vectors from 0.5?

The squares of the z-scores average to 1 (the SD is 1), so the vector's length is \(\sqrt{n}\). Then \(\mathbf{z}_x\cdot\mathbf{z}_y/n\) is the dot product of two vectors of length \(\sqrt{n}\) divided by \(n\), which is the cosine of the angle between them. So \(r\) is the cosine similarity of the two standardised columns.

A friend says that a p-value of 0.04 means there is a 96% chance model B is better. What is wrong, and what would you say instead?

The p-value assumes the models are equal and gives how often luck would produce a result this lopsided: about 4% of the time. The p-value does not give the probability that either model is better. Say: if the models were equal, a gap this large would be unusual, and then give the size of the gap with an interval.
